claims.text: The overall high-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is governed by their ability to form an adherent, ultra-nanocrystalline oxide layer during thermal exposure and sliding.
The self-generated tribo-oxide acts as a lubricating, load-bearing film.
The tribo-oxide impedes direct metal-to-metal contact and thereby reduces friction and wear rate.
The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating is polycrystalline, has a relatively coarse initial grain structure, and has minimal surface oxidation.
The proposed intervention is pre-oxidation in air at 700°C for 30 minutes before wear testing.
The intervention is compared with an otherwise equivalent as-deposited coating receiving no pre-treatment.
Wear testing is to be performed at approximately 700°C under moderate-to-high normal loads in sliding contact.
Pre-oxidation produces a nanocrystalline oxide scale at the coating surface.
The proposed surface oxide scale is likely enriched in chromium- and copper-based oxides.
Thermal exposure during pre-oxidation or in-service wear promotes controlled surface oxidation.
Thermal exposure and sliding promote dynamic recrystallization at the coating surface.
Controlled oxidation and dynamic recrystallization result in a continuous ultrafine oxide layer.
The ultrafine oxide layer reduces friction by acting as a lubricious barrier.
The oxide layer reduces material loss by protecting the underlying alloy from severe plastic deformation and abrasion.
The pre-oxidized coating will have a significantly lower friction coefficient than the untreated coating.
The pre-oxidized coating will have a significantly lower wear rate than the untreated coating.
Post-wear microscopy and spectroscopy will reveal a uniform, adherent, ultra-nanocrystalline oxide layer on the pre-oxidized coating.
The proposed mechanism is applicable near 700°C and under loads typical of high-temperature sliding contact.
Outside the stated temperature and loading window, other wear mechanisms may dominate.
Failure to obtain statistically significant friction and wear-rate improvements, or failure to observe a continuous adherent ultra-nanocrystalline oxide layer, would falsify the hypothesis.
